title: Simultaneous improvement of hydrogen embrittlement resistance and tensile strength of quenching and partitioning steel through dense multiple interfaces
abstract: As the third generation of advanced high-strength steel, quenching and partitioning (QP) steel faces a severe issue of hydrogen embrittlement (HE). In-situ slow strain rate tensile tests (SSRT) were conducted to compare the HE resistance of QP980 and QP1180, and it was found that QP1180 had better HE resistance as well as higher strength. The microstructure of the materials was characterized using scanning electron microscopy (SEM), X-ray diffraction (XRD), electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD), and transmission electron microscopy (TEM). Also, hydrogen traps were investigated using thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) and hydrogen permeation tests combined with microstructure analysis. Results indicate that hydrogen was predominantly trapped at interfaces. Specifically, the number of hydrogen traps at the interface of QP1180 was one order of magnitude higher than that of QP980. Dense multiple interfaces including dense interfaces (the main hydrogen trap sites) and novel chemical boundaries (between the areas with high Mn and low Mn content) in QP1180 help to mitigate local and overall hydrogen accumulation, which effectively alleviates hydrogen-induced cracking and prevents the early formation of large-size cracks. Therefore, QP1180 shows better HE resistance as well as higher strength.
